opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What stood out most was the speed. Things moved incredibly fast. You'd have an idea in the morning, and by the afternoon people expected to see it running, or at least a prototype with real numbers. There wasn't much patience for long planning documents or layers of approval. The default was: try it, measure it, and decide based on what you see.

Related to that, the teams were very flat and small for the scale of what they were building. You didn't have a lot of people whose only job was coordination. Engineers owned things end to end. If you worked on inference, you weren't just writing a kernel and handing it off. You were thinking about the serving system, the cluster, how it affected training and product, all of it. That's demanding, but it's also a huge learning opportunity, because you see the whole stack and understand how your piece fits.

The intensity was real too. People worked very hard, and the bar was high. Some people love that and some find it difficult to sustain, so I think it's important to be honest that it's not for everyone. For me, coming from a research and open-source background, working on systems like SGLang, it was eye-opening to see how much a small, focused group can ship when everyone is aligned on a clear goal and the iteration loop is very short.

If I had to sum it up: urgency, ownership, and a strong bias toward building over discussing. Those are lessons I've carried with me since.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not convey an expectation that office politics inevitably emerge as a company grows.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that stood out most was just how flat and fast everything was. There was almost no layer between the people writing code and the decisions being made. If you had an idea, you didn't write a doc and wait two weeks for a review cycle. You tried it, and if it worked, it shipped. That kind of ownership is rare at a company that size.

The flip side is that it was intense. People were genuinely in the office a lot, and the expectation was that you cared about the outcome as much as anyone else did. It's not a place where you can coast. But for the people who thrive on that, it was very energizing, because you could see your work matter within days instead of quarters.

The other thing I'd mention is how much the infrastructure and research teams were intertwined. Coming from the open-source systems side, I was used to a lot of separation between the people building serving systems and the people training models. At xAI those lines were much blurrier. Everyone was expected to understand the whole stack to some degree, which honestly made the engineering better, because you weren't optimizing for a problem you only half understood.
